solution:
**Animal husbandry.**

The chapter gives this as the second head of its commercial applications: 'Animal Husbandry - Two main methods as artificial insemination and embryo transfer are used in animal husbandry. It helps to improve both, the quantity and quality of animal products. Ex. Milk, meat, wool, etc.' It adds that animals with more strength have been developed for hard work by the same route.

(The exercise prints 'embryo transplant' where the chapter's own sentence says 'embryo transfer'; both name the same method.)

**Stem cell research.**

The chapter says it in exactly these words: 'In biotechnology, stem cell research is a revolutionary event after cloning. This technique has the potential of bringing about the fundamental changes in the medical science.'

**Diabetes.**

The chapter's human-health section states that 'The hormone insulin is used in treatment of diabetes', and its box of proteins produced by biotechnology pairs 'Insulin - Diabetes'. The same passage explains that insulin was earlier collected from the pancreas of horses, and that nowadays it is prepared with the help of bacteria into whose genome the human insulin gene has been inserted.

**Pisciculture (fish farming).**

The chapter states: 'Government of India has vowed to increase the production by encouraging the people for pisciculture by launching the program "Nil-Kranti Mission-2016" (NKM-16). 50% to 100% subsidies are offered in this case.'

It files this under the blue revolution, which it defines as 'Production of various useful aquatic organisms with the help of water'.

| Column A | Column B |
|---|---|
| a. Interferon | 3. Viral infection |
| b. Factor (VIII) | 5. Haemophilia |
| c. Somatostatin | 2. Dwarfness |
| d. Interleukin | 4. Cancer |

All four pairs are taken from the chapter's own box, which invites the reader to 'See the proteins produced by biotechnology and the names of diseases they are used against' and then lists: Insulin - Diabetes, Somatostatin - Dwarfism, Erythropoietin - Anaemia, Factor VIII - Haemophilia, Interleukin - Cancer, Interferon - Viral infection.

**Option 1. Diabetes is left over.** It belongs to insulin, which this exercise does not list among the four items in Column A.

Note that the exercise prints item b as a bare 'Factor', while the chapter prints it in full as 'Factor VIII'. The pairing is unaffected, because haemophilia is the only disease left for it.

Corrected statement: **Changes in genes of the cells are brought about in genetic technique.**

The chapter separates the two techniques where it lists the main areas of biotechnology: 'Use of genetic and non-genetic technique. Non-genetic biotechnology involves use of either cell or tissue. Ex. Tissue culture, production of hybrid seeds, etc.'

So the non-genetic technique works with whole cells or tissues and does not touch the genes. Altering genes belongs to the genetic technique, which the same list describes as 'Development of plants, animals and products of desired quality by gene manipulation', with the production of human growth hormone using genetically modified bacteria as its example.

Corrected statement: **Gene from Bacillus thuringiensis is introduced into cotton.**

The chapter gives this as Bt Cotton: 'A gene had been isolated from the bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis and integrated with the genome of cotton. Due to this, the toxin which is fatal for bollworm was produced in leaves and bolls of cotton. If bollworm feeds on leaves, the toxin destroys its alimentary canal and the bollworm dies.'

The only other crop the chapter names for this gene is brinjal - 'Bt Brinjal variety is developed by using the gene isolated from Bacillus thuringiensis. This improved variety of brinjal kills the pest in same way as the Bt cotton does' - so 'brinjal' is equally correct. **Soyabean is not mentioned anywhere in this chapter**, which is what makes the printed statement wrong.

The chapter presents biotechnology as a working field in two ways: the areas in which it is applied commercially, and the institutions that teach it and carry out its research.

**The fields of work it names**

| Field | What is done in it, in the chapter's words |
|---|---|
| Crop biotechnology | Hybrid seeds, genetically modified crops (Bt cotton, Bt brinjal, Golden Rice), herbicide tolerant varieties, biofertilizers, tissue culture |
| Animal husbandry | Artificial insemination and embryo transfer, to improve the quantity and quality of milk, meat and wool |
| Human health | Diagnosis of disease, production of insulin, somatotropin and blood clotting factors, vaccines, interferon, gene therapy, cloning |
| Industrial products (white biotechnology) | Industrial chemicals by less expensive processes, e.g. alcohol from sugar molasses using transgenic yeast |
| Environment | Bioremediation, treatment of sewage and solid waste, cleaning of oil spillage |
| Food biotechnology | Bread, cheese, wine, beer, yoghurt and vinegar produced with the help of microorganisms |
| DNA fingerprinting | Establishing the identity of a person from available DNA, 'mainly useful in forensic sciences' |

**Where this work is done and taught**

The chapter records that the 'Government of India had established the National Biotechnology Board in 1982. This board was transformed into department of biotechnology under the ministry of science and technology, in 1986.' Working under that department it names the National Institute of Immunology, the National Facility for Animal Tissue and Cell Culture, the National Centre for Cell Science, the National Brain Research Centre and the Central Institute of Medicinal and Aromatic Plants, and says of them: 'There are facilities of higher education and research in these institutes from where thousands of students have pursued Ph.D. degrees and are contributing to the progress of country in the field of biotechnology.'

Alongside these it names, for crop research, the 'Indian Agricultural Research Institute (IARI), New Delhi, National Citrus Research Institute, Nagpur and allied branches, Indian Institute of Sciences, National Pomegranate Research Institute, Solapur'; the Center for DNA fingerprinting and Diagnostics, Hyderabad for forensic work; and the National Center for Cell Science, Pune and 'Instem', Bengaluru for research on cells.

[Note: the chapter does not print a list of job designations. It describes the fields in which biotechnology is applied and the institutes where a student may study and work, and this answer is confined to those.]

The chapter makes the case for medicinal plants under 'Cultivation of Medicinal Plants':

1. **They are the basis of a living tradition of treatment.** 'India has been gifted with a great biodiversity. Indian citizens have established the humble and strong relation with the nature. We have a great tradition of ayurveda that cures the diseases with the help of natural sources.'
2. **Their medicinal value lies in a definite active ingredient.** The chapter's own chart gives the pattern:

| Local name of plant | Name of active ingredient | Uses |
|---|---|---|
| Adulsa | Vasicine present in the leaves | Cough |

3. **They are becoming rare, which is why they must now be grown deliberately.** 'During earlier days, medicinal plants were collected from the forest. However, due to depletion in forest area, medicinal plants are becoming rare. Hence, medicinal plants are being cultivated.'
4. **They are important enough to have a national institute of their own.** Among the institutes working under the department of biotechnology the chapter names the Central Institute of Medicinal and Aromatic Plants.

The two plants the chapter shows are Adhatoda vasica (Adulsa) and Azadirachta Indica (Neem).

This is to be answered from your own daily use; the products the chapter names as coming from biotechnology are these:

| Kind of product | What the chapter names |
|---|---|
| Food | Bread, cheese, wine, beer, yoghurt and vinegar - 'produced with the help of microorganisms. These food items are probably the oldest ones produced with the help of biotechnology'; also yoghurt from milk and alcohol from molasses |
| Medicines | Insulin for diabetes, antibiotics, vaccines, interferon, and hormones such as somatotropin and blood clotting factors |
| Vaccines | Polio and hepatitis vaccines, made more thermo-stable by biotechnology |
| Food crops | Golden Rice (a variety developed in 2005 carrying 23 times more beta carotene), hybrid seeds and other genetically modified crops |
| Cotton | Bt cotton, made resistant to bollworm |
| Milk and milk products | The dairy products of the white revolution |
| Fish and other aquatic food | Rohu, catla, shrimp and lobsters cultured on a large scale under the blue revolution |

So the products of biotechnology in ordinary daily use are chiefly the fermented foods (bread, cheese, yoghurt, vinegar), the vaccines and medicines one has been given, the milk products, and the food grains, vegetables and cotton cloth grown from improved varieties.

**The chapter does not print a list of precautions to be taken while spraying pesticides.** What it does say about pesticides, and the precautions that follow directly from it, are these:

1. **Keep the use under control, and use them only when the plant's own defence is not enough.** 'Though the natural immunity of plants can prevent the infections, use of insecticides is not under control.'
2. **Remember that a pesticide is a poison, and that it does not stay where it is sprayed.** 'Pesticides are in fact a type of poison. This poison enters the food-web through water and food and its bio-magnification occurs.' The chapter also records that 'These poisonous chemicals reached the human body through food and water and their adverse harmful effects on human and environment became apparent.' So the spray must be kept out of food and drinking water.
3. **Avoid the ones already proved dangerous.** 'Various pesticides like DDT, malathion, chloropyriphos, etc. have been proved to be dangerous.'
4. **Do not destroy the farmer's natural helpers.** 'Irrespective of the natural friends of farmers like frogs and insectivorous birds, pesticides are used on large scale for increase in yield.'
5. **Prefer the alternatives the chapter recommends** - biopesticides and biofertilizers, which it lists among the new concepts in biotechnological methods, and organic farming, which 'includes complete ban on chemical fertilizers and pesticides and use of local, sturdy varieties and thereby maintaining natural balance'.

[Note: this chapter names no precaution about protective clothing, masks, wind direction or dosage. Those are sensible practical precautions but they are not stated in this chapter, so they are not claimed here.]

Some organs are the most valuable because the body has only one of them, life cannot continue without them, and they cannot be replaced except by transplantation.

The chapter puts the loss first: 'Various organs in the human body either become less efficient or completely functionless due to various reasons like aging, accidents, infections, disorders, etc. Life of such person becomes difficult or even fatality may occur under such conditions. However, if a person gets the necessary organ under such conditions, its life can be saved.'

It then separates what a living person can spare from what he cannot:

| Can be donated during life time | Can be donated after death only |
|---|---|
| One kidney - 'As the process of excretion can occur with the help of single kidney, person can donate another one' | Liver, heart, eyes - 'other organs cannot be donated during life time' |
| Skin from certain parts of the body | |

That is exactly the measure of their value. A paired organ like the kidney, or a tissue like skin, can be given away and the donor still lives; the single organs cannot, so for the patient who has lost one there is no source but a donor after death - which is why the chapter says 'Life of many people can be saved by organ and body donation. Blinds can regain the vision. Life of many people can be rendered comfortable by donation of organs like liver, kidneys, heart, heart valves, skin, etc.'

Their value is also recognised in law: the chapter records that organ donation and transplantation are 'under the control of "Transplantation of Human Organs Act, 1994" and subsequent amendments of 2009, 2011 and 2014 so that overall process would be transparent and any person would not be cheated.'

Fruit processing matters because fruit is a perishable crop and processing is what makes it last and keeps it in daily use.

1. **Fruit is perishable, so it would otherwise be wasted.** 'Fruits are perishable agro-produce. It needs the processing in such a way that it can be used throughout the year.'
2. **It makes a seasonal fruit available all the year round** - that is the purpose the chapter states for the processing.
3. **It gives the products we use every day.** 'We are daily using various products prepared from fruits. All are consuming the products like chocolates, juices, jams and jellies. All these products can be produced by processing on fruits.'
4. **It is done by a range of ordinary methods**, so it can be carried out at every scale: 'Fruit processing includes various methods ranging from storage in cold storage to drying, salting, air tight packing, preparing murabba, evaporating, etc.'

The chapter illustrates it with a mango processing unit (fig. 8.14) and asks the reader to look for fruit processing industries in his own surroundings.

**Vaccination is the giving of a vaccine** - and the chapter defines a vaccine exactly: 'Vaccine is the "antigen" containing material given to acquire either permanent or temporary immunity against a specific pathogen or disease.'

So vaccination means introducing that antigen-containing material into the body so that the immune system is made ready in advance against a particular pathogen, and the person acquires immunity - permanent or temporary - against that disease before ever meeting it.

The chapter also describes how the material itself has changed:

- **Traditionally**: 'vaccines were prepared with the help of pathogens. Completely or partially killed pathogens were used as vaccines. However, due to this, there were chances of contracting the disease in case of some persons.'
- **Now**: 'scientists produced the antigen in laboratory with the help of gene isolated from the pathogen and used it as vaccine. Thus, safer vaccines are being produced.' And: 'proteins which act as antigen are injected in pure form instead of injecting the killed or semi-killed pathogens. These proteins keep the persons away from the diseases by keeping the immune system active. Thus, injecting the antigens is safest way in vaccination.'

Such vaccines 'are more thermo-stable and remain active for longer duration', the chapter's examples being the vaccines of polio and hepatitis. It adds that edible vaccines are being worked on, in the form of transgenic potatoes which would generate immunity against cholera and the disease caused by E. coli when eaten raw.

The eight boxes are filled with the merits of biotechnology. The chapter's own section headed **Benefits of Biotechnology** gives the first four:

| No. | Merit of biotechnology |
|---|---|
| 1 | The per hectare yield can be increased irrespective of the limitations of crop-land area |
| 2 | Expenses on disease control are minimised, since disease resistant varieties have been developed |
| 3 | Yield per annum has increased, through varieties that set fruit fast |
| 4 | Stress resistant varieties have become possible, which withstand variable temperature, water stress and changing fertility of the soil |
| 5 | Medicines and hormones are produced - insulin, somatotropin, blood clotting factors and interferon, made with the help of bacteria and transgenic E. coli |
| 6 | Safer vaccines are produced from antigens made in the laboratory; they are more thermo-stable and stay active longer, and edible vaccines are being developed |
| 7 | Diseases are diagnosed early and quickly - diabetes and heart disease even before symptoms appear, AIDS and dengue within a few minutes - and gene therapy can treat a genetic disorder such as phenylketonuria |
| 8 | Environmental problems are solved - bioremediation, treatment of sewage and solid waste, and cleaning of oil spillage with oil-digesting bacteria - and biofertilizers replace chemical fertilizers |

Any eight merits drawn from the chapter will do. Others it offers are DNA fingerprinting for forensic work, cloning and stem cell therapy in medicine, industrial chemicals made cheaply with transgenic yeast, and better quality and quantity of milk, meat and wool through animal husbandry.

[Note: the chapter's section actually titled 'Benefits of Biotechnology' lists only the first four. The remaining four here are taken from elsewhere in the same chapter, because the printed chart has eight boxes.]

The three blank circles are filled from the chapter's section **Uses of Stem Cells**, which gives regenerative therapy in two parts and organ transplantation as the third:

| Circle | Use of stem cells | What the chapter says |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Cell therapy | 'Stem cells are used to replace the dead cells in case of conditions like diabetes, myocardial infarction, Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, etc.' |
| 2 | Production of blood cells | 'To produce blood cells required in conditions like anaemia, thalassemia, leukemia, etc.' |
| 3 | Organ transplantation | 'In case of failure of organs like kidney and liver, those can be produced with the help of stem cells and transplanted.' |

All three rest on the one property the chapter states at the start: stem cells 'give rise to all other types of cells present in the body of multicellular organisms', and if collected before differentiation begins and cultured with a biochemical stimulus 'they can transform themselves into desired type of cells, thereby tissues and finally into organs'.

The chapter mentions two further uses outside this list: stem cells 'play an important role in wound healing', and in therapeutic cloning stem cells are derived from a cell made by uniting a somatic cell nucleus with an enucleated egg cell, so that 'various diseases can be treated with the help of these stem cells'.

**Cancer.**

The correlation runs protein : disease it is used against. The chapter's box of proteins produced by biotechnology gives 'Insulin - Diabetes' and 'Interleukin - Cancer'.

**Viral infection.**

The correlation runs protein : disease it is used against. The chapter's box gives 'Interferon - Viral infection' and 'Erythropoietin - Anaemia'. The chapter describes interferon separately as well: 'This is a group of small sized protein molecule used in treatment of viral diseases... nowadays, with the help of biotechnology, transgenic E. coli are used for production of interferon.'

[Textbook note: the chapter's box of proteins produced by biotechnology prints 'Somatostatin - Dwarfism', and this correlation is keyed to that box. The chapter's own treatment section on the previous page instead names somatotropin - 'Biotechnology is useful for production of hormones like insulin, somatotropin and blood clotting factors' - so the two pages do not agree on which of the two hormones belongs against dwarfness. The answer below follows the box, because that is the list this exercise is drawn from.]

**Somatostatin.**

The correlation runs protein : disease it is used against, and the chapter's box gives 'Somatostatin - Dwarfism' alongside 'Factor VIII - Haemophilia'.

**Fishery - the production of useful aquatic organisms (pisciculture).**

The chapter defines the term: 'Production of various useful aquatic organisms with the help of water is called as blue revolution.' As the white revolution belongs to dairy, the blue revolution belongs to fish farming: 'Marine and fresh water fishery is possible on large scale. Fresh water fishes like rohu, catla and other fishery products like shrimp and lobsters are being cultured on large scale.'

The chapter adds that the Government of India encourages pisciculture through the programme 'Nil-Kranti Mission-2016' (NKM-16), offering 50% to 100% subsidies.

**Usefulness of biotechnology, as the chapter records it**

| Field | Usefulness |
|---|---|
| Agriculture | Hybrid seeds; genetically modified crops such as Bt cotton, Bt brinjal and Golden Rice; herbicide tolerant varieties; biofertilizers (Rhizobium, Azotobacter, Nostoc, Anabaena, Azolla); tissue culture, by which 'genetic improvement of the plants has become possible' |
| Yield and cost | Higher yield per hectare irrespective of the land available, lower spending on disease control through resistant varieties, higher yield per annum through fast fruit setting varieties, and stress resistant varieties that withstand temperature, water stress and poor soil |
| Animal husbandry | Artificial insemination and embryo transfer, improving both the quantity and the quality of milk, meat and wool |
| Human health | Early and rapid diagnosis - diabetes and heart disease before symptoms, AIDS and dengue within minutes; insulin made by bacteria carrying the human insulin gene; somatotropin, blood clotting factors and interferon; safer and more thermo-stable vaccines; gene therapy for a disorder such as phenylketonuria; cloning and stem cell therapy |
| Industry | Industrial chemicals by cheaper processes, e.g. alcohol from sugar molasses with transgenic yeast |
| Environment | Bioremediation, treatment of sewage and solid waste, and cleaning of oil spillage by oil-digesting bacteria |
| Food | Bread, cheese, wine, beer, yoghurt and vinegar |
| Forensic science | DNA fingerprinting, by which 'identity of the criminal can be established with the help of any part of its body found at the site of crime' |

**Harmfulness of biotechnology, as the chapter records it**

The chapter states one, and it is about cloning: 'Controlling the inheritance of hereditary diseases, continuation of generations, enhancing the specific tendency may become possible due to cloning technique. **However, there is world-wide opposition to human cloning on various issues.**'

Two further cautions can be read from it. The older way of making a vaccine, from completely or partially killed pathogens, carried 'chances of contracting the disease in case of some persons' - a risk that biotechnology removed rather than created, by producing the antigen in the laboratory instead. And of the edible vaccine the chapter itself asks what will happen if the transgenic potatoes are cooked before they are eaten, which points to a real limitation of that method.

**The comparison**

Set side by side, the chapter is overwhelmingly on the side of usefulness: it devotes whole sections to agriculture, animal husbandry, health, industry, the environment, food and forensic science, and only a single sentence to a harm - the worldwide opposition to human cloning. Its own summing up is that 'There is considerable progress mainly in the field of agriculture and pharmacy due to biotechnology.'

[Note: the chapter's other warnings - that chemical fertilizers and pesticides poison food and water, that DDT, malathion and chloropyriphos bio-magnify through the food web, and that liberal use of chemical fertilizers decreases the fertility of the soil - are attributed to chemical farming, not to biotechnology. The chapter offers biofertilizers, biopesticides and organic farming as the answer to those harms. They are therefore not counted here as harms of biotechnology, and no harm beyond the one the chapter states is claimed.]
